In 1830, only a few miles away from what is now the great city of Cincinnati, lay an immense and almost unbroken forest. <break time="0.8s" /> The restless pioneers who had first settled the region soon pushed farther west, but a few of them remained, and Murlock was one of these. <break time="0.8s" /> He lived alone in a small log house surrounded on all sides by the forest, of whose gloom and silence he seemed to be a part. <break time="0.8s" /> He was never known to smile or to waste a word, and he supported himself by hunting and by selling animal skins in the river town. <break time="0.8s" /> His cabin had a single door and, directly opposite, a single window, but the window was boarded up, and nobody could remember a time when it was not. <break time="0.8s" /> Nobody knew why it was closed, and it was certainly not because he disliked the light, for passing hunters often saw him sunning himself on his doorstep. <break time="0.8s" /> I believe there are few persons living today who know the secret of that window, but I happen to be one of them, as you shall see. <break time="0.8s" /> Murlock was said to be about fifty, yet with his white hair, his long white beard, and his deeply lined face, he looked closer to seventy.

His gray eyes were dull and lifeless, and his face was marked with so many wrinkles that he seemed much older than his years. <break time="0.8s" /> I first heard his story from my grandfather, who had known Murlock well when both of them were living near that great forest. <break time="0.8s" /> One day Murlock was found dead in his cabin, and since it was not a time of coroners and newspapers, people simply agreed that he had died naturally. <break time="0.8s" /> He was buried beside the grave of his wife, who had died so many years before that the settlers remembered almost nothing about her. <break time="0.8s" /> Many years later, as a bold boy, I crept up to the ruined cabin, threw a stone at it, and ran from the ghost that every boy in the area knew haunted the place. <break time="0.8s" /> Long before, when Murlock built his cabin, he was young, strong, and full of hope, and he had brought a young wife with him from the East. <break time="0.8s" /> Her name and character are not recorded, yet she seems to have been a woman worthy of his love, cheerfully sharing the dangers and hardships of his life. <break time="0.8s" /> There is reason to believe that they loved each other deeply, and that the memory of her held Murlock to that lonely place for the rest of his life.

One day Murlock returned from hunting and found his wife ill with a fever, so confused in her mind that she did not even recognize him. <break time="0.8s" /> There was no doctor within miles and no neighbor to call, and since she could not be left alone, he had no choice but to care for her himself. <break time="0.8s" /> For three days he nursed her alone, but on the third day she sank into unconsciousness and passed away, apparently without ever coming back to her senses. <break time="0.8s" /> From what we know of a nature like his, we may venture to fill in some of the details of the picture that my grandfather drew. <break time="0.8s" /> When he was convinced that she was dead, Murlock had sense enough to remember that the dead must be prepared for burial. <break time="0.8s" /> In performing this sacred duty, he made mistakes now and then, did certain things incorrectly, and did others which he had done correctly over and over again. <break time="0.8s" /> He was surprised that he did not weep, and he felt a little ashamed of it, for surely it is unkind not to weep over the dead. <break time="0.8s" /> Tomorrow, he said aloud, I shall have to make the coffin and dig the grave, but things cannot be so bad as they seem.
